def: A small gram-negative coccobacillus carried in the mouths of cats and dogs. It causes rapidly developing cellulitis and sometimes osteomyelitis after bites or scratches.

An antistaphylococcal penicillin resistant to staphylococcal beta-lactamase, used against methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Resistance (MRSA) arises from altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a, encoded by mecA.

A first-generation cephalosporin used for surgical prophylaxis and for skin and soft-tissue infections from staphylococci and streptococci. It has little activity against anaerobes or most gram-negative rods.
A calcium-activated phosphatase in T cells that dephosphorylates NFAT so it can enter the nucleus and drive IL-2 transcription. It is the target of cyclosporine and tacrolimus.

Blood in the pleural space, usually from chest trauma or rib fracture injuring intercostal or lung vessels. It causes dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds and is drained with a chest tube.
A taxane chemotherapy drug that stabilizes microtubules and blocks their disassembly, arresting cells in mitosis (M phase). Toxicities include myelosuppression and peripheral neuropathy.
Hardy, environmentally resistant spore-like forms shed in feces by protozoa such as Cryptosporidium and Toxoplasma. Ingesting them from contaminated water or cat feces transmits infection.
A genus of small gram-negative intracellular coccobacilli. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia, acquired from rabbits, ticks or deer flies, with ulceroglandular disease and lymphadenopathy.
A tick-borne infection of red blood cells by Babesia, transmitted by Ixodes ticks in the Northeast US. It causes hemolytic anemia and fever, with ring forms and "Maltese cross" tetrads on smear.
A genus of mosquitoes that transmit yellow fever, dengue, Zika and chikungunya viruses. Aedes aegypti and albopictus bite during the day.
Ultrasound combining real-time B-mode imaging of a vessel with Doppler measurement of blood flow velocity. It is used to detect deep vein thrombosis, arterial stenosis and flow abnormalities.

Infection and inflammation of the fetal membranes and amniotic fluid, usually from ascending vaginal bacteria after membrane rupture. It causes maternal fever, uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia.

An enveloped positive-strand RNA flavivirus (genus Hepacivirus) spread by blood. It frequently causes chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, and is treated with direct-acting antivirals.
Antiretroviral drugs such as raltegravir and dolutegravir that block HIV integrase, preventing the viral DNA from inserting into the host genome.

A full-thickness tear of the esophagus, most often from endoscopy or from forceful vomiting (Boerhaave syndrome). It leaks air and gastric contents into the mediastinum, causing mediastinitis and subcutaneous emphysema.
A fetal position in which the buttocks or feet, rather than the head, enter the pelvis first. Frank breech (hips flexed, knees extended) is the most common type.
A family of enveloped, filamentous negative-strand RNA viruses including Ebola and Marburg. They cause hemorrhagic fever with high mortality.
A rodent-borne bunyavirus spread by inhaling aerosolized urine or droppings. In the Americas it causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, with fever and rapid noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.
A herpesvirus that causes roseola infantum, a high fever in infants that ends as a rash appears. It can cause febrile seizures and reactivate after transplantation.

Narrowing of the pulmonary valve that obstructs right ventricular outflow. It produces a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border, often with a click, and can cause right ventricular hypertrophy.

A spore-forming, anaerobic gram-positive rod that causes tetanus. Its toxin, tetanospasmin, blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA, glycine) in the spinal cord, causing spastic paralysis and lockjaw.
The perforated part of the ethmoid bone forming the roof of the nasal cavity. Olfactory nerve fibers pass through it, so fracture can cause anosmia and CSF rhinorrhea.
A protozoan transmitted by the tsetse fly that causes African sleeping sickness. T. brucei gambiense and rhodesiense invade the CNS and evade immunity by varying their surface glycoproteins.
A hypersensitivity skin reaction with target (bullseye) lesions, most often triggered by herpes simplex virus or Mycoplasma, sometimes by drugs. It is milder than Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
G protein-coupled receptors for histamine. H1 mediates allergic and vasodilatory effects, H2 stimulates gastric acid secretion by parietal cells, and H3 and H4 act in the CNS and immune cells.
The movement of stomach contents into the duodenum. It is slowed by fat, acid and cholecystokinin, and delayed in gastroparesis.

Drugs such as omeprazole that irreversibly block the H+/K+ ATPase of gastric parietal cells, strongly reducing acid secretion. They treat GERD and ulcers; long use risks C. difficile infection and low magnesium.
The H+/K+ ATPase on the apical membrane of gastric parietal cells that secretes hydrogen ions into the stomach lumen in exchange for potassium. It is the target of omeprazole-type drugs.

Drugs such as spironolactone and eplerenone that block the mineralocorticoid receptor in the collecting duct, causing potassium-sparing diuresis. Spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia and gynecomastia.

Excess androgen levels or effects in women, causing hirsutism, acne and irregular menses. Common causes include polycystic ovary syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia and androgen-secreting tumors.
A decrease in the number of receptors or amount of a gene product in response to a stimulus, often prolonged exposure to an agonist, which lowers the cell's responsiveness.
Four small glands behind the thyroid that secrete parathyroid hormone, raising serum calcium. Chief cells make PTH; they derive from pharyngeal pouches 3 (inferior) and 4 (superior).

Reduced blood flow to the brain that deprives neurons of oxygen and glucose, causing infarction if prolonged. Global hypoperfusion injures watershed areas and vulnerable neurons in the hippocampus and cortex.
A hormone made by the stomach that stimulates appetite through hypothalamic neurons. Levels rise before meals and with sleep deprivation, and are high in Prader-Willi syndrome.
A tumor or tangled overgrowth of nerve tissue. Traumatic neuromas form after nerve injury, and Morton neuroma is perineural fibrosis of a plantar digital nerve causing forefoot pain.

Diabetes drugs ending in -gliflozin that block sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 in the proximal tubule, causing glucosuria. They lower glucose, protect heart and kidney, and risk genital yeast infections and euglycemic ketoacidosis.
A coiled tube on the back of the testis where sperm mature and are stored. Epididymitis presents with scrotal pain and often follows chlamydia or gonorrhea in young men.
Paired glands behind the bladder that add fructose-rich fluid, making most of the volume of semen. They join the vas deferens to form the ejaculatory duct.
Coiled tubules in the testis where spermatogenesis occurs. Sertoli cells line them and support germ cells, while Leydig cells lie in the surrounding interstitium.
Testing during pregnancy for fetal disorders, using ultrasound, maternal serum markers, cell-free DNA, chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis.
The complete set of chromosomes of a cell, arranged by size and banding pattern for study. It detects aneuploidy such as trisomy 21 and large translocations.
A congenital defect in which the urethral opening is on the underside of the penis rather than the tip. It results from incomplete fusion of the urethral folds.
A 0 to 10 rating of a newborn at 1 and 5 minutes based on heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability and color. Low scores signal need for resuscitation.

Precancerous changes of cervical squamous cells from HPV infection, graded as low-grade (LSIL, mild dysplasia) or high-grade (HSIL, moderate to severe dysplasia, more likely to progress to carcinoma).
Dilated, fragile submucosal vessels of the gut, typically the right colon in older adults. It causes painless lower GI bleeding and is associated with aortic stenosis.
A malignancy of epidermal keratinocytes arising on sun-exposed skin, often from actinic keratosis. Histology shows keratin pearls; it can metastasize.
A germ cell tumor that secretes alpha-fetoprotein, common in young children (sacrococcygeal or testis) and in young women. Histology shows Schiller-Duval bodies.
Finger-like projections of the fetal placenta that bathe in maternal blood and exchange gases and nutrients. Chorionic villus sampling takes them for prenatal genetic testing.
Swelling of tissue from impaired lymphatic drainage, due to obstruction, filariasis, surgical node removal or radiation. It produces non-pitting, firm swelling of a limb.
The vessel in the umbilical cord that carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. After birth it becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver.
Loss of the sense of smell, from olfactory nerve damage, head trauma, viral infection or Kallmann syndrome. Hyposmia is a partial loss.

A usually benign bone tumor of young adults occurring at the epiphysis of long bones, especially around the knee. Histology shows multinucleated giant cells; the classic radiograph is a soap-bubble lesion.
The laboratory process of staining and arranging a cell's chromosomes to detect abnormal number or structure.

DNA repair that cuts out damaged bases and fills the gap. Base excision repair fixes single altered bases; nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions such as thymine dimers and is defective in xeroderma pigmentosum.
A group of skin disorders marked by dry, thick, scaly skin resembling fish scales. Ichthyosis vulgaris is caused by filaggrin mutations and is common with atopy.
Short sequences of DNA (1 to 6 base pairs) repeated in tandem. Instability from defective mismatch repair is seen in Lynch syndrome.

An autosomal recessive disorder from ATM gene mutation causing defective DNA double-strand break repair. It features cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias, immunodeficiency with low IgA and increased cancer risk.
Addition of a hydroxyl (OH) group to a molecule. In collagen, hydroxylation of proline and lysine requires vitamin C, and its failure causes scurvy.
A protease that digests elastin. Neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar walls when unopposed by alpha-1 antitrypsin, causing emphysema; pancreatic elastase aids protein digestion.
A laboratory test that detects an antigen or antibody using an enzyme-linked antibody that produces a color change. It is commonly used for HIV screening.

The forebrain fails to split into left and right halves early in development, causing midline face defects (single central incisor, close-set eyes, cleft lip; cyclopia when severe). Linked to Sonic hedgehog mutations, trisomy 13 and fetal alcohol exposure.
A preexcitation syndrome in which an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) bypasses the AV node. ECG shows a short PR interval and delta wave; it predisposes to reentrant tachycardia.
A granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of the aortic arch and its branches in young Asian women. It causes weak or absent pulses in the arms and visual or neurologic symptoms.
High blood pressure with no identifiable secondary cause, accounting for most cases. It is driven by genetic and lifestyle factors and raises the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney damage.
Hardening and thickening of the arterial wall with loss of elasticity. Types include atherosclerosis, Monckeberg medial calcification and hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
Abnormal dilation of the thoracic aorta, linked to cystic medial degeneration (Marfan syndrome), hypertension, and tertiary syphilis. Risk is dissection or rupture.
Zinc-dependent enzymes that degrade extracellular matrix such as collagen. Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are involved in tissue remodeling, wound healing and tumor invasion.
Chest pain at rest from transient coronary artery vasospasm, with transient ST elevations. It is treated with calcium channel blockers and nitrates and is made worse by triptans and cocaine.
An anthracycline chemotherapy drug that intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, used in acute myeloid leukemia. Cardiotoxicity is a major adverse effect.
A fusion protein of the TNF receptor and IgG Fc that binds and neutralizes TNF-alpha. It treats rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis and raises risk of reactivated tuberculosis.
Particles left after lipoprotein lipase strips triglycerides from chylomicrons. They carry dietary cholesterol to the liver, taken up via ApoE receptors.
A cofactor on chylomicrons and VLDL that activates lipoprotein lipase. Its deficiency causes severe hypertriglyceridemia.
A gram-negative diplococcus that causes otitis media, sinusitis and COPD exacerbations. It produces beta-lactamase, so it is often resistant to ampicillin.
The anterior prominence of the lower jaw (chin) formed by the mandible.
The gene encoding epidermal growth factor receptor, a receptor tyrosine kinase promoting cell growth. Mutations or overexpression occur in lung cancer, and are targeted by erlotinib and cetuximab.

An autoimmune disease with antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing acetylcholine release. It causes proximal weakness that improves with use and is associated with small cell lung cancer.
Sudden constriction of the smooth muscle of the bronchi, causing wheezing and difficulty breathing. It is seen in asthma and anaphylaxis and treated with beta-2 agonists.
A network of nerves formed from the C5 to T1 roots that supplies the upper limb. It is organized as roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches.
A tumor of thymic epithelial cells in the anterior mediastinum, associated with myasthenia gravis, pure red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinemia.
Obstruction of the superior vena cava, usually by lung cancer or lymphoma, causing facial and arm swelling, distended neck veins and dilated chest wall collaterals.
A procedure in which a needle is inserted into the pleural space to remove fluid for diagnosis or relief of dyspnea. It is done above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.

A disorder from deficient ADAMTS13 causing platelet-rich microthrombi. It features microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, kidney dysfunction and neurologic signs; treatment is plasma exchange.
The glycolytic enzyme that converts phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate, producing ATP. Its deficiency causes hemolytic anemia because red cells depend on glycolysis.
Inability to digest lactose due to lactase deficiency in the brush border. It causes bloating, watery diarrhea and gas after dairy.
Glycogen storage disease type V from muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. It causes exercise cramps, myoglobinuria and no rise in lactate during ischemic exercise.
An alkylating agent used before bone marrow transplant and for chronic myeloid leukemia. Toxicities include pulmonary fibrosis and hyperpigmentation.
Drugs such as naloxone and naltrexone that block opioid receptors, reversing opioid overdose or reducing craving.
A long-acting opioid receptor antagonist used to treat opioid and alcohol use disorder. It can precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients and may cause hepatotoxicity.
A muscarinic agonist that stimulates secretions and contracts the ciliary muscle and pupil. It is used for glaucoma and dry mouth, and in the challenge test for cystic fibrosis (sweat test).
A disorder of C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causing excess bradykinin and episodes of non-itchy swelling of the face, airway and gut. ACE inhibitors can trigger attacks, and C4 is low.
Sudden, strong urge to urinate with involuntary leakage, from detrusor overactivity. It is treated with antimuscarinic drugs.
The thick tendon of the gastrocnemius and soleus attaching to the calcaneus. Rupture causes a positive Thompson test; fluoroquinolones raise tendinopathy risk.
A lysosomal storage disease. Type A and B result from sphingomyelinase deficiency, with hepatosplenomegaly, foam cells and, in type A, a cherry-red macula and neurodegeneration.
An X-linked urea cycle defect that causes hyperammonemia with elevated orotic acid and low BUN. It presents with vomiting, lethargy and neurologic injury.
A purine analog that inhibits de novo purine synthesis, used for acute leukemia and inflammatory bowel disease. It is metabolized by xanthine oxidase, so allopurinol raises its toxicity.
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, a purine salvage enzyme that converts hypoxanthine and guanine back to nucleotides. Its absence causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
An X-linked recessive disorder from HGPRT deficiency, causing purine overproduction. It features hyperuricemia and gout, intellectual disability, dystonia and self-mutilating behavior.
A nonpurine inhibitor of xanthine oxidase used to lower uric acid in chronic gout. It carries a cardiovascular death warning.

Chronic amnesia from thiamine deficiency, usually in alcohol use disorder, with confabulation and anterograde and retrograde memory loss. It follows Wernicke encephalopathy and involves the mammillary bodies.
Absorptive epithelial cells lining the small intestine, with brush border microvilli that absorb nutrients and secrete enzymes.
Tapeworms, flat segmented parasites that live in the intestine. Examples are Taenia solium, Taenia saginata, Diphyllobothrium latum and Echinococcus.
Blood cell production outside the bone marrow, in organs such as spleen and liver, occurring in myelofibrosis and severe chronic anemias. It causes hepatosplenomegaly.
An antimalarial that eradicates the dormant liver hypnozoites of Plasmodium vivax and ovale. It can cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
The most rostral part of the forebrain, forming the cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia and hippocampus.
The most caudal embryonic brain vesicle, which becomes the medulla oblongata.
Brainstem nuclei at the pontomedullary junction that receive input from the inner ear and control eye movement, balance and posture.

A small infarct of a deep penetrating artery, usually caused by hypertension and lipohyalinosis. It affects the internal capsule, basal ganglia, thalamus or pons and causes pure motor or sensory deficits.
A tuberculosis drug that blocks arabinosyl transferase, preventing cell wall synthesis. It can cause optic neuritis, with loss of red-green color vision.
Degranulation of mast cells and basophils that frees histamine, causing vasodilation, itching, bronchoconstriction and increased vascular permeability.
Regulatory proteins whose levels rise and fall through the cell cycle and activate cyclin-dependent kinases to drive progression. Abnormal cyclin D1 is seen in mantle cell lymphoma.
A fatal prion disease causing rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus and spongiform change of the brain. Variant CJD is linked to eating contaminated beef.
Meningeal inflammation with lymphocytic CSF and negative bacterial cultures, most often viral (enteroviruses). It is usually milder and self-limited.
Longitudinal tears of the gastroesophageal mucosa from forceful vomiting, typically in alcohol use. It causes hematemesis after retching.
Protrusion of part of the stomach through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm. The sliding type is most common and is associated with GERD.
The giant intestinal roundworm, acquired by swallowing eggs from contaminated soil. Larvae pass through the lungs; adults can cause intestinal or biliary obstruction.
A genus of large intestinal roundworms; Ascaris lumbricoides infects humans via fecal-oral egg ingestion.
A fracture of the skull base, causing raccoon eyes, mastoid ecchymosis (Battle sign), hemotympanum and CSF otorrhea or rhinorrhea.
A flavivirus spread by Aedes mosquitoes and sexual contact. Infection in pregnancy causes microcephaly; it can also trigger Guillain-Barre syndrome.
A highly contagious disease caused by the variola virus, with a centrifugal rash of uniform vesicles and pustules. It was eradicated in 1980.
A monoclonal antibody against vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) that blocks tumor angiogenesis. It is used for colorectal, lung and other cancers and in wet macular degeneration.
A short-acting benzodiazepine metabolized by direct glucuronidation, making it safer in liver disease and the elderly.

A rare life-threatening reaction to volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine, with abnormal calcium release via the ryanodine receptor. It causes rigidity, fever and hypercarbia; treated with dantrolene.
Bone density below normal but not low enough for osteoporosis (T-score between -1 and -2.5).
A low-potency first-generation antipsychotic that blocks dopamine D2 receptors. It causes sedation, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension and QT prolongation.
A drug used for influenza A and Parkinson disease. It blocks viral M2 ion channels and increases dopamine release; side effects include livedo reticularis.
Bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia of a newborn with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. It causes lethargy, seizures, deafness and choreoathetoid cerebral palsy.
Flatworms, or flukes, such as Schistosoma, Clonorchis and Paragonimus.
A mosquito-borne flavivirus infection causing fever, jaundice and hemorrhage. Councilman bodies are seen in the liver.
The immune response carried out by T cells rather than antibodies, targeting intracellular pathogens, tumors and transplants.
A type III hypersensitivity reaction 1 to 2 weeks after exposure to foreign protein or certain drugs, with fever, rash, arthralgia and low complement from immune complex deposition.
Skin inflammation from contact with an irritant or allergen. Allergic contact dermatitis is type IV hypersensitivity (poison ivy, nickel).
Drugs that dampen immune activity to prevent transplant rejection or treat autoimmune disease, such as cyclosporine, tacrolimus, azathioprine and mycophenolate.
A seronegative inflammatory arthritis in patients with psoriasis. It has asymmetric joint involvement, dactylitis, nail pitting and pencil-in-cup deformity.
The narrow part of the femur between head and shaft. Fractures can disrupt the medial circumflex femoral artery and cause avascular necrosis.
A superficial skin infection by Malassezia causing hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly patches. KOH shows "spaghetti and meatballs" hyphae and yeast.
A monobactam antibiotic active against gram-negative rods but not gram-positives or anaerobes. It is safe in penicillin allergy.
Immunosuppressants such as cyclosporine and tacrolimus that block calcineurin and reduce IL-2 production by T cells. They cause nephrotoxicity.
A calcineurin inhibitor that binds FKBP12 and blocks T-cell IL-2 transcription. It is used in transplants; toxicities include nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity and diabetes.
An early set of nonspecific symptoms preceding the main features of an illness.
A curved gram-negative rod, a common cause of bloody diarrhea from undercooked poultry. It can lead to Guillain-Barre syndrome and reactive arthritis.
The disseminated form of Mycobacterium leprae infection with weak cell-mediated immunity (Th2 response), causing diffuse skin nodules, leonine facies and many bacilli.
An oral prodrug of ganciclovir used for CMV infections. It inhibits viral DNA polymerase and causes bone marrow suppression.
The pork tapeworm. Eating undercooked pork causes intestinal infection; ingesting eggs causes cysticercosis with neurocysticercosis and seizures.
A fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Side effects include tendon rupture, QT prolongation and cartilage damage in children.
A procedure passing a catheter into heart chambers or coronary arteries to measure pressures and perform angiography or intervention.
Abnormal formation of the hip joint in which the femoral head is unstable or dislocated. Screening uses the Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers.
A calicivirus and a leading cause of outbreaks of acute viral gastroenteritis, with vomiting and watery diarrhea. It spreads on cruise ships.
Cationic antibiotics such as colistin that disrupt gram-negative outer membranes. Toxicities are nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
A spore-forming gram-positive rod causing food poisoning, notably from reheated rice. The emetic form begins within hours; the diarrheal form follows in about 8 to 16 hours.
Alteration of surface antigens by microbes to evade immune detection, as in influenza, trypanosomes, Borrelia and gonococci.
The protozoan causing Chagas disease, spread by reduviid ("kissing") bugs. It causes cardiomyopathy, megaesophagus and megacolon.
A squamous cancer arising in the nasopharynx, strongly linked to EBV and common in Southeast Asia and southern China. It presents with neck nodes.
A herpesvirus (HHV-5) causing congenital infection and opportunistic disease in the immunocompromised. Owl's-eye intranuclear inclusions are seen.
The spirochete causing Lyme disease, transmitted by Ixodes ticks. It causes erythema migrans, facial palsy and arthritis.
A nucleotide analog that inhibits viral DNA polymerase, used for CMV retinitis and acyclovir-resistant herpesviruses. Nephrotoxicity is the main risk.
The synapse between a motor neuron and skeletal muscle fiber, where acetylcholine acts on nicotinic receptors. It is affected in myasthenia gravis.
A potent long-acting glucocorticoid, given to mothers at risk of preterm delivery to speed fetal lung maturity.
A 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetic for chemotherapy and postoperative nausea. It can prolong the QT interval.
Delayed stomach emptying without obstruction, causing early satiety, nausea and vomiting. Diabetes is the commonest cause.
An aminoglycoside poorly absorbed from the gut, used for bowel prep and hepatic encephalopathy. It is ototoxic and nephrotoxic if absorbed.
A guanosine analog antiviral for hepatitis C and RSV. It causes hemolytic anemia and is teratogenic.
Liver inflammation lasting more than 6 months, from hepatitis B or C, autoimmunity or alcohol. It can progress to cirrhosis.
A hormone released by atrial myocytes in response to stretch. It promotes natriuresis and vasodilation, lowering blood pressure.
Pituitary hormones, LH and FSH, that regulate the gonads. Placental hCG acts like LH.
Heat production by the body, as through brown fat uncoupling protein (thermogenin) or shivering.
A life-threatening exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis with fever, tachycardia, agitation and altered mental status. It is treated with propranolol, propylthiouracil and steroids.
The first steroid in steroidogenesis, made from cholesterol by the enzyme desmolase (side-chain cleavage), and the precursor of all steroid hormones.
The rate-limiting enzyme of glycogen synthesis, adding glucose to growing chains. Insulin activates it; glucagon and epinephrine inhibit it.
A pituitary tumor producing excess ACTH, causing Cushing disease with hypercortisolism. High-dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol.
Forward bulging of the eyeball, classically in Graves disease from orbital tissue expansion.
The continuous resorption of old bone by osteoclasts and formation of new bone by osteoblasts.
Sampling cells from a mass with a thin needle for cytologic evaluation, commonly used for thyroid nodules and lymph nodes.

Acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone, made in liver mitochondria from fatty acids during fasting or insulin deficiency. They fuel the brain in prolonged fasting and cause ketoacidosis when excess.
A pancreatic alpha-cell tumor causing hyperglycemia and necrolytic migratory erythema, weight loss and diarrhea.
A membrane antiporter that exchanges extracellular sodium for intracellular hydrogen ions, regulating intracellular pH.
A growth factor that stimulates neutrophil production, given to recover white cells after chemotherapy (filgrastim).
Diabetes and weight loss drugs such as liraglutide and semaglutide that mimic GLP-1, increasing insulin, suppressing glucagon and slowing gastric emptying. They risk pancreatitis.
A potent androgen made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase, important for male external genitalia and prostate growth.
The first half of the menstrual cycle, in which FSH drives follicle growth and estrogen rises.
A nerve (S2-S4) supplying the perineum, external anal sphincter and external urethral sphincter. It can be blocked in childbirth near the ischial spine.
A malignant skeletal muscle tumor of childhood. The embryonal type, sarcoma botryoides, appears in the vagina or bladder; desmin is positive.
A benign tumor of fibrous connective tissue.
Agents that cause congenital malformations when exposed during pregnancy, such as thalidomide, isotretinoin, alcohol and warfarin.
An antidepressant that blocks serotonin 5-HT2 receptors, used for depression and insomnia. It can cause priapism.
A breast cancer with E-cadherin loss, producing single-file cell infiltration and often bilateral multifocal disease.
The presence in one person of two or more cell lines with different genetic makeup, arising from postzygotic mutation or nondisjunction.
Fusion of the lower poles of the kidneys across the midline, trapped by the inferior mesenteric artery. It is associated with Turner syndrome.
A drug combining a sulfa antibiotic and 5-aminosalicylic acid, used in ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis. It can cause sulfa allergy and reversible infertility in men.
A translation factor that moves the ribosome along mRNA in eukaryotes. Diphtheria toxin inactivates it by ADP-ribosylation.
Mucus-secreting epithelial cells in the gut and airway.
The protein subunit of microtubules, a target of colchicine, vinca alkaloids, taxanes and mebendazole.
The main sterol of fungal cell membranes, the target of amphotericin B and nystatin; azoles inhibit its synthesis.
The most abundant collagen, found in bone, skin and tendon. Defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta.
The proportion of people with a given genotype who show the phenotype.
Expansion of three-base DNA repeats that causes diseases such as Huntington disease and fragile X syndrome.
Connective tissue fibers of elastin and fibrillin that give recoil to skin and arteries. Fibrillin mutations cause Marfan syndrome.
A dilation at the carotid bifurcation containing baroreceptors that monitor blood pressure via the glossopharyngeal nerve.
A fast heart rhythm originating above the ventricles, often AV nodal reentry, with a narrow QRS. Vagal maneuvers and adenosine treat it.
A tiny capillary outpouching, seen in diabetic retinopathy as retinal dots, and in hypertension (Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms).
A small-vessel vasculitis in children with IgA immune complexes, causing palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain and nephritis.
